facts.label: Credit analysis of the data
facts.text: Net leverage on trailing reported EBITDA rose to 6.04x at 2026-09-30 from 5.73x at the 2025 year-end and 4.10x a year earlier, even though net debt is lower than at either year-end, because earnings have fallen faster than debt. The mechanism is fuel: fuel and related taxes rose by USD 4,427 million in the first nine months of 2026 while revenue grew 15.63%, so operating income fell to USD 535 million from USD 1,042 million. For creditors the consequence is that deleveraging so far has come from cash rather than earnings, and a further rise in fuel prices would widen the gap before any debt is repaid. The strongest contrary evidence is liquidity, with USD 11,763 million available and nothing drawn on the revolving facilities, which would have to be spent down before leverage becomes a refinancing problem. Basis: calculation C13; calculation C31; calculation C29; calculation C24; 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 25; 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 31

facts.label: Credit analysis of the data
facts.text: A large part of the balance sheet is customer-funded. Air traffic liability of USD 9,414 million, loyalty program liability of USD 11,514 million and fuel financing of USD 933 million together stand at USD 21,861 million, USD 3,225 million above the year-end. Ticket and mileage cash is received before service and reverses as flights are flown, so it flatters operating cash flow in the build season and becomes a call on cash in a downturn, particularly because the filings warn that credit card processing terms can tighten if financial condition worsens. The float sits outside Total Debt and bears no interest, but it is a claim on future cash. facts.label: Credit analysis of the data
facts.text: American is a net lender to its parent. Net related-party receivables of USD 10,430 million comprise USD 12,512 million due from the parent less USD 2,082 million owed to the parent's regional subsidiaries, and the annual report links growth in the parent receivable to American providing cash for the parent's financing. None of this is cash and it is outside net debt here. Creditors of American therefore hold a buffer that depends on the parent's ability to repay, while the parent carries USD 3,746 million of its own unsecured promissory notes. facts.label: Contrary evidence and what would change the view
facts.text: The strongest evidence against a moderate governance view is the size of the parent exposure: the net receivable from related parties exceeds American's own equity, and the parent's consolidated accounts show a stockholders' deficit of USD 4,224 million, so American's positive equity depends on a claim on a group that does not itself carry book equity. A second challenge is litigation, where the Northeast Alliance antitrust class action is at the certification stage and the American Eagle accident actions were still being filed when the annual report was written, both without an estimate of amount in the sources; the issuer reports industry-standard insurance for the accident. facts.text: In February 2026 the AAdvantage issuers amended the term loan agreement and cut the margin on the 2025 AAdvantage term loan. In March 2026 American extended its three main revolving facilities to March 2031, raising aggregate commitments from USD 3.0 billion to USD 3.1 billion, and extended a smaller USD 350 million revolver to March 2028. facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: - Earnings, not the debt balance, are the weak link. Net debt fell by USD 1,820 million between the 2025 year-end and 2026-09-30, but trailing EBITDA fell by USD 479 million, so net leverage rose to 6.04x from 5.73x and cover of interest paid fell to 2.06x from 2.19x. The cause is fuel, which rose by USD 4,427 million in nine months against revenue growth of 15.63%, so operating margin fell to 1.14% from 2.56%. Basis: calculation N01; calculation N02; calculation N03; calculation N04; calculation N05; calculation N06; Financial foundation (CP-1)

facts.label: Key findings

facts.label: Strengths and weaknesses
facts.text: Strengths. The first is liquidity: USD 11,763 million is available with no revolver drawing and facility maturities extended to 2031, which gives time to absorb a fuel or demand shock. The second is loyalty and co-brand income at 13.82% of FY2025 revenue, a stream less tied to fares than ticket sales, although it is pledged to AAdvantage lenders. The third is policy: no dividends or buybacks in 2025 or 2024 and no sponsor. The fourth is maturity management in 2026, including the 2014 term loan moved to May 2033, which removed a January 2027 maturity. The fifth is scale: a mainline fleet of which 54.00% is owned and a hub network that management says is carrying premium and corporate growth. Basis: calculation N08; calculation N16; calculation N17; Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 100

facts.label: Business, ownership and revenue drivers
facts.text: American is a major network carrier that sells scheduled passenger and cargo transportation through nine hubs, buys regional capacity from wholly-owned and third-party carriers at fixed fees, and earns a loyalty and co-brand income stream alongside ticket revenue. The credit link is mixed: passenger travel is 83.49% of FY2025 revenue and is discretionary and cyclical, so cash-flow visibility comes mainly from the 13.82% loyalty share and from advance ticket sales, and refinancing confidence rests on a secured funding market that American used repeatedly in 2026. facts.text: Costs are largely fixed or outside management control in the short run. facts.label: Competitive and macro forces
facts.text: Rivalry is intense and sets pricing, because carriers match fare cuts quickly and ultra-low-cost carriers press fares in many markets, which limits margin recovery when costs rise. The threat of new entrants is moderated by hub, slot and gate constraints that the annual report describes and by aircraft supply, and substitutes matter mainly on short segments where ground and rail compete. Buyer power sits with corporate accounts and online travel agents that control distribution and its cost, and supplier power is high because a limited number of manufacturers supply aircraft and engines, delaying deliveries or raising fleet cost, while unions and fuel suppliers set the two largest costs. facts.label: Competitive and macro forces
facts.text: Macro and policy factors are material here, unlike in many sectors. Conflict in the Middle East and Ukraine has contributed to oil price volatility, which feeds straight into fuel cost, and a prolonged government shutdown, regulation of routes and slots, and antitrust litigation over the Northeast Alliance can each change earnings or cash. These matter to credit because fuel is the main cause of the margin squeeze and because litigation cash calls compete with debt service. facts.label: Financial profile and outlook
facts.text: The financial profile reads as follows, dimension by dimension. Scale and market position are strong, with a mainline fleet of more than 1,000 aircraft and revenue of USD 54,626 million in FY2025. Competitive advantage and business diversification are average, because hubs and loyalty income are offset by fare competition and a domestic base. Cost and capex flexibility, margin stability and free cash flow stability are weak, for the reasons above. Ability to refinance is average: secured access is proven but the issuer carries a non-investment grade rating, and USD 7,861 million falls due in 2028. Liquidity is strong at USD 11,763 million. Financial policy and governance are average, because payouts are conservative while the parent receivable is large and legal capacity is unread. Basis: calculation N08; calculation N10; calculation N06; Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 33

facts.text: The scenario is a prolonged fuel shock rather than a recession. The initiating condition is fuel staying near the outlook price of about USD 4.70 per gallon through 2027 while growth slows, as management expects. The first operational break is that unit revenue gains fade but fuel, labour and fixed regional fees do not, so operating margin falls below 1.14% and EBITDA below the trailing USD 2,916 million; each ten cents per gallon adds about USD 450 million to group annual fuel cost. Financial transmission follows: net leverage rises above 6.04x, cover falls below 2.06x, and free cash flow stays negative while aircraft deliveries continue and the customer-funded float of USD 21,861 million reverses in a slower season. facts.text: The liquidity consequence is that USD 11,763 million of liquidity covers the USD 11,411 million of principal due in 2027 and 2028 only 1.03x, with cash also needed for operations, so a card processor holdback would matter. Management levers are real: capital expenditure and deliveries can be cut, as they were in 2026, aircraft certificates have repeatedly funded deliveries, sale-leasebacks have yielded USD 77 million in nine months, and repayment of part of the USD 10,430 million receivable by the parent is a possible lever although its terms are not established. Resilience appears sufficient to avoid liquidity distress through 2027 on stated liquidity, but the 2028 maturities of USD 7,861 million would need earnings recovery or continued secured market access, and an observable trigger is the refinancing of the 2028 notes and loans before leverage rises further. No default is assumed. facts.label: Overall credit view
facts.text: Overall, American presents an adequate business profile supported by liquidity, loyalty income, extended maturities and conservative payouts, but credit quality is constrained by fuel-driven margin compression, net leverage of 6.04x on derived EBITDA, a USD 10,430 million receivable from its parent and a largely pledged asset base. Cash-flow durability appears weak because trailing free cash flow is a deficit of USD 132 million. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on fuel prices and continued secured market access ahead of USD 7,861 million due in 2028. The primary downside path is a prolonged fuel shock on fixed labour, regional and fleet costs. Further analysis would require ratings, executed debt documents, the proxy statement and the intercompany terms. Fundamental credit completed. Top risk: sustained fuel cost without margin recovery. ## Findings
### Bottom line

The seven supplied documents are enough to start a credit snapshot of American Airlines, Inc. on its own accounts, because every annual and quarterly report prints the subsidiary's statements apart from its parent's, so creditors can be judged at the borrower's own perimeter. The parent's group figures and all three earnings presentations describe American Airlines Group Inc. only, so they serve as context and never as the issuer's own numbers.

## Request

## Findings
### Bottom line

American Airlines, Inc. carries net debt of 6.04x trailing reported EBITDA with interest cover of only 2.06x, so creditors rely on liquidity of USD 11,763 million rather than earnings while fuel costs depress profit. Net debt was USD 17,623 million at 2026-09-30, USD 1,820 million below the 2025 year-end, yet leverage rose from 5.73x because trailing EBITDA fell by USD 479 million. These are American's own figures; the parent's group figures are context only.
Basis: calculation C04; calculation C13; calculation C14; calculation C15; calculation C24; 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 26; 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 201

Two definitions limit the ratios. Reported EBITDA is derived from operating income and the depreciation line on the face of the statement, which omits depreciation booked in other lines, and American holds a USD 12,512 million net receivable from its parent that is not cash and is excluded from net debt. The parent's reported net debt of USD 28,079 million includes lease and pension obligations and is not comparable.
Basis: calculation C05; calculation C23; calculation C39; 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 40; EX-99.2_2026-10-22_earningspresentation.htm.jsonl, page 10; Source readiness (CP-0)
### Credit analysis of the data

Net leverage on trailing reported EBITDA rose to 6.04x at 2026-09-30 from 5.73x at the 2025 year-end and 4.10x a year earlier, even though net debt is lower than at either year-end, because earnings have fallen faster than debt. The mechanism is fuel: fuel and related taxes rose by USD 4,427 million in the first nine months of 2026 while revenue grew 15.63%, so operating income fell to USD 535 million from USD 1,042 million. For creditors the consequence is that deleveraging so far has come from cash rather than earnings, and a further rise in fuel prices would widen the gap before any debt is repaid. The strongest contrary evidence is liquidity, with USD 11,763 million available and nothing drawn on the revolving facilities, which would have to be spent down before leverage becomes a refinancing problem.
Basis: calculation C13; calculation C31; calculation C29; calculation C24; 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 25; 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 31

Cover of cash interest by reported EBITDA is 2.06x trailing against 2.19x for FY2025 and 2.53x for FY2024. Interest paid is falling, at USD 1,416 million trailing against USD 1,551 million for FY2025, so the squeeze comes from earnings rather than from rates or new debt. Accrued interest expense exceeded interest paid by USD 187 million over the first nine months of 2026, so cash-based cover flatters cover on accrued interest.
Basis: calculation C14; calculation C37; 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 26; 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 27; 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 254

Operating cash flow of USD 4,440 million for the first nine months is double the USD 2,229 million of a year earlier, but the quarterly report attributes the rise mainly to working capital in the air traffic and loyalty liabilities and to the 2025 cash funding of the parent's note settlement, partly offset by lower profitability. Free cash flow of USD 1,780 million for the nine months therefore reflects seasonal and intercompany timing rather than earnings power; over the trailing twelve months it is a deficit of USD 132 million after capital expenditure of USD 4,273 million.
Basis: calculation C22; calculation C09; calculation C10; 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 26; 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 63

Liquidity is USD 11,763 million, made up of USD 8,253 million of cash and short-term investments and USD 3,510 million of undrawn facilities, equal to 0.45x of balance-sheet debt. The undrawn amount is the issuer's printed availability under three revolving facilities and two smaller facilities, one of which, a USD 50 million cargo receivables facility, expires in December 2026. The filings state a covenant requiring at least USD 2.0 billion of unrestricted cash and cash equivalents plus undrawn revolver amounts; its definition differs from the liquidity measure used here, so no covenant headroom is calculated.
Basis: calculation C15; calculation C33; 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 31; 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 60; 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 61

A large part of the balance sheet is customer-funded. Air traffic liability of USD 9,414 million, loyalty program liability of USD 11,514 million and fuel financing of USD 933 million together stand at USD 21,861 million, USD 3,225 million above the year-end. Ticket and mileage cash is received before service and reverses as flights are flown, so it flatters operating cash flow in the build season and becomes a call on cash in a downturn, particularly because the filings warn that credit card processing terms can tighten if financial condition worsens. The float sits outside Total Debt and bears no interest, but it is a claim on future cash.
Basis: calculation C32; 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 26; 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 30; 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 3

American is a net lender to its parent. Net related-party receivables of USD 10,430 million comprise USD 12,512 million due from the parent less USD 2,082 million owed to the parent's regional subsidiaries, and the annual report links growth in the parent receivable to American providing cash for the parent's financing. None of this is cash and it is outside net debt here. Creditors of American therefore hold a buffer that depends on the parent's ability to repay, while the parent carries USD 3,746 million of its own unsecured promissory notes.
Basis: calculation C39; 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 40; 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 15; 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 257

Reported EBITDA is a derived figure, built from the depreciation line on the face of the income statement. The cash flow statement shows depreciation and amortization of USD 2,177 million for FY2025 against USD 1,884 million on the face, which would raise FY2025 EBITDA by USD 293 million to USD 3,688 million and lower FY2025 leverage to 6.85x from 7.44x. The face-of-statement basis is used for every period because the quarterly statements print no total depreciation, so the series is consistent but overstates leverage and understates cover. The issuer states no adjusted EBITDA for American, so no adjusted ratios are shown.
Basis: calculation C05; calculation C23; 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 201; 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 202

No financing event after 2026-09-30 is stated in the sources up to the cutoff, so no pro forma net debt is shown. The quarterly report mentions the exercise of purchase options for five Airbus A320 aircraft in October 2026, which adds to aircraft commitments but not to net debt.

# AMERICAN AIRLINES, INC. — Business & governance
## Request

Business and governance fact base for the credit snapshot pathway, as of 2026-11-05, for AMERICAN AIRLINES, INC. The scope is the business, ownership, operating model, transactions and governance facts that matter to creditors, taken from the 2025 annual report, the three 2026 quarterly reports and the three earnings presentations. No acquisition or sponsor transaction is stated in the sources, so the transaction summary covers financings.

## Findings
### Bottom line

American is a scaled network airline whose creditors face fuel, labour and parent-funding risk rather than sponsor risk, because it is wholly owned by a widely held parent that paid no dividends and bought back no shares in 2025 or 2024. The main governance exposure is that American has lent USD 12,512 million net to that parent, with repayment terms not established.
Basis: calculation K06; calculation K07; 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 102; 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 103; 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 40

The 2026 refinancings pushed the main revolving facilities out to March 2031 and the 2014 term loan to May 2033, but they also placed junior debt on aircraft that were already financed. Director, executive and ownership detail and the executed debt documents are not in the sources, so legal capacity to pay dividends or move assets is not established.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 32; 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 34; 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 264; Source readiness (CP-0)
### Key findings

- The franchise is a hub network carrier whose cyclical passenger core is cushioned by loyalty income. Passenger travel is 83.49% of FY2025 revenue and loyalty and co-brand card revenue 13.82%, and cash from card and other partners was USD 6.2 billion in 2025, so a stream that does not move with fares or fuel sits beside revenue that does.
Basis: calculation K01; calculation K03; 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 13; 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 211

- The most defensive revenue stream is also the most encumbered. The AAdvantage notes and term loans of USD 5,985 million are secured by a first-priority interest in the program agreements and payments and are guaranteed by the parent and special-purpose subsidiaries, so loyalty cash is first available to those lenders and only then to other creditors.
Basis: calculation K04; 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 31; 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 227

- There is no sponsor or controlling shareholder in the sources, so extraction risk rests on financial policy, which has been conservative on payouts. The parent paid no cash dividends and made no share repurchases in 2025 or 2024, foreign ownership is capped at 24.9% of votes and 49.0% of equity, and a tax benefit plan penalises any holder of 4.9% or more; the parent is widely held rather than sponsor owned.

- The parent relationship is the principal governance exposure. American's net related-party receivable of USD 10,430 million is larger than its stockholder's equity of USD 8,895 million, and the annual report ties its growth to American providing cash for the parent's financing, including the 2025 settlement of the parent's convertible notes; repayment terms, security and interest are not established in the sources.
Basis: calculation K06; calculation K07; calculation K08; 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 40; 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 257

- The 2026 financing extended maturities and lowered margin but added encumbrance. The main revolving facilities now mature in March 2031, the 2014 term loan was refinanced to May 2033, and the margin on the 2025 AAdvantage term loan fell by 0.50 percentage points; against that, USD 870 million was borrowed junior to existing equipment notes on aircraft already financed, and new aircraft and engine certificates added further secured debt.

- Fuel and labour dominate the cost base and neither is hedged or fixed. Fuel expense rose to USD 12,444 million in the first nine months of 2026 from USD 8,017 million with no fuel hedges, the group estimates USD 45 million of annual fuel cost for each one cent per gallon, and most employees are unionised under agreements several of which become amendable in 2027.

Basis: calculation K09; calculation K10; 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 25; 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 45; 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 69; 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 19; 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 253
### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest evidence against a moderate governance view is the size of the parent exposure: the net receivable from related parties exceeds American's own equity, and the parent's consolidated accounts show a stockholders' deficit of USD 4,224 million, so American's positive equity depends on a claim on a group that does not itself carry book equity. A second challenge is litigation, where the Northeast Alliance antitrust class action is at the certification stage and the American Eagle accident actions were still being filed when the annual report was written, both without an estimate of amount in the sources; the issuer reports industry-standard insurance for the accident.

What would change the view is evidence on the receivable: repayment terms, security, subordination or any restriction on upstream cash in the debt documents would move the assessment toward lower risk, while a deferral, a write-down or a further large advance would move it toward higher risk. An adverse class certification ruling, a dividend or buyback restart before leverage falls, or a sponsor or large holder emerging in the proxy statement would also change it.
### Limitations

- Director, executive, compensation and ownership detail is incorporated from a proxy statement that was not supplied, so the conclusion that there is no controlling shareholder rests on the absence of a disclosed holder and would change if a large holder were disclosed.

- No executed debt documents were supplied, so the view on parent support and extraction rests on behaviour and not on legal capacity, and a restricted-payments or intercompany-transfer limit in those documents could change it.

- The business description in the annual report covers American and its parent together, so network, passenger and regional fleet figures describe the combined operation and may overstate American's own scale in the business conclusion.
- Capacity, unit revenue and unit cost are printed for the group only, so the conclusion on fuel and cost sensitivity uses group measures as a proxy for American.
- Passenger revenue by region is incomplete for the nine months of 2026 in the text supplied, so the revenue mix conclusion uses FY2025 and the third quarter of 2026 only.

### Transaction summary and new debt issues

No acquisition, sponsor buyout, recapitalisation or change of control involving American is stated in the sources. The transactions in the period are financings: amendments and extensions of existing facilities, refinancings, and new secured borrowings against aircraft and engines, set against prepayments of older debt.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 257; 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 36; Source readiness (CP-0)

In February 2026 the AAdvantage issuers amended the term loan agreement and cut the margin on the 2025 AAdvantage term loan. In March 2026 American extended its three main revolving facilities to March 2031, raising aggregate commitments from USD 3.0 billion to USD 3.1 billion, and extended a smaller USD 350 million revolver to March 2028. In May 2026 it refinanced the 2014 term loan of about USD 1.1 billion, moved its maturity from January 2027 to May 2033, added USD 703 million and priced the loans at 3.00% over SOFR, with annual repayment of 1.00% from May 2027.

New secured borrowing in the first nine months of 2026 came mainly from aircraft and engine financings, which the group reports at about USD 4.1 billion of proceeds. They were a USD 870 million junior borrowing in March on aircraft already financed, aircraft certificates of about USD 1.1 billion in May, engine certificates of USD 567 million in June that refinanced USD 228 million of maturing 2019 certificates, aircraft certificates of about USD 1.3 billion in August of which about USD 633 million was held in escrow at the quarter end and is not reported as debt, and USD 705 million of equipment loans at variable rates averaging 5.87%.

Against these, American repaid USD 629 million of a senior short-term term loan, prepaid USD 1.0 billion of the 8.50% senior secured notes and prepaid USD 310 million of equipment notes. The creditor consequence is mixed: maturities are longer and margins lower, but more aircraft and engines are pledged and some new debt ranks behind existing equipment notes, which reduces the unencumbered asset base available to later or unsecured creditors.

# AMERICAN AIRLINES, INC. — Fundamental credit
## Request

Fundamental credit assessment for the credit snapshot pathway, as of 2026-11-05, for AMERICAN AIRLINES, INC. The scope is American's own business, financial profile, parent relationship, downside path and monitoring triggers, built on the supplied filings and the Source readiness, Financial foundation and Business & governance outputs. No rating, relative value, covenant, recovery or sizing conclusion is drawn.

## Findings
### Bottom line

American's credit rests on liquidity and long-dated secured funding rather than earnings, because fuel has cut operating margin to 1.14% and lifted net leverage to 6.04x, leaving creditors exposed to a further fuel shock and to the parent's ability to repay USD 10,430 million.
Basis: calculation N06; calculation N01; calculation N13; Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A)

Liquidity of USD 11,763 million with nothing drawn on the revolving facilities, extended maturities and no shareholder payouts give time, but USD 7,861 million of principal falls due in 2028 and trailing free cash flow is a deficit of USD 132 million, so deleveraging depends on fuel prices easing before the 2028 maturities.
Basis: calculation N08; calculation N10; calculation N11; Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 65
### Key findings

- Earnings, not the debt balance, are the weak link. Net debt fell by USD 1,820 million between the 2025 year-end and 2026-09-30, but trailing EBITDA fell by USD 479 million, so net leverage rose to 6.04x from 5.73x and cover of interest paid fell to 2.06x from 2.19x. The cause is fuel, which rose by USD 4,427 million in nine months against revenue growth of 15.63%, so operating margin fell to 1.14% from 2.56%.
Basis: calculation N01; calculation N02; calculation N03; calculation N04; calculation N05; calculation N06; Financial foundation (CP-1)

- Liquidity is the main support and it is long-dated. USD 11,763 million is available, including USD 3,510 million undrawn, and the three main revolving facilities now run to March 2031; that is 1.03x the USD 11,411 million of principal due in 2027 and 2028, although the same cash also funds operations and the customer-funded float.
Basis: calculation N08; calculation N09; Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 31; 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 32

- Refinancing is manageable but concentrated in 2028. USD 7,861 million, or 30.74% of principal, falls due in 2028, and all of American's principal is secured, so refinancing depends on continued access to the aircraft certificate market that American used repeatedly in 2026.
Basis: calculation N10; calculation N19; 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 31; 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 65; Business & governance (CP-1A)

- Cash conversion is weak. Operating cash flow of USD 4,141 million over the trailing twelve months was less than capital expenditure of USD 4,273 million, a free cash flow deficit of USD 132 million; the USD 1,780 million surplus for nine months reflects seasonal liabilities and the absence of a 2025 outflow to the parent, and aircraft commitments continue.
Basis: calculation N11; Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 63; 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 64

- The asset base is increasingly pledged, which limits flexibility for later creditors. AAdvantage financing of USD 5,985 million is secured on loyalty assets, and in 2026 American borrowed USD 870 million junior to existing equipment notes on aircraft already financed; management's claim of unencumbered assets and first-lien capacity above USD 26 billion is a group-level figure that the sources do not verify for American.

Basis: calculation N12; Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 31; 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 34; EX-99.2_2026-10-22_earningspresentation.htm.jsonl, page 6

- The parent is a credit exposure as well as an owner. American's net receivable from related parties of USD 10,430 million is 1.17x its stockholder's equity of USD 8,895 million, the parent reports a stockholders' deficit of USD 4,224 million, and repayment terms are not established; against that, the parent paid no dividends and made no buybacks in 2025 or 2024.
Basis: calculation N13; Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 8; 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 40

- The franchise supports revenue but does not insulate earnings from fuel. Loyalty and co-brand revenue was 13.82% of FY2025 revenue and 54.00% of the mainline fleet is owned, yet the company holds no fuel hedges, and the group estimates USD 45 million of annual fuel cost for each one cent per gallon.
Basis: calculation N16; calculation N17; Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 45; 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 69
### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest case against this cautious view is that the earnings squeeze is a fuel shock on a franchise that is growing: revenue rose 15.63% in nine months, management reports premium revenue up 22.9% and loyalty enrolments up 27.4% at group level, and it guides to fourth-quarter group revenue growth of 19.5% to 22.5% on a fuel price of about USD 4.70 per gallon. Liquidity is higher than at either earlier year-end, the loss is concentrated in one cost line, and federal tax losses of about USD 11.7 billion shield cash taxes, so a retreat in fuel prices would restore margin quickly.

Basis: EX-99.2_2026-10-22_earningspresentation.htm.jsonl, page 5; EX-99.2_2026-10-22_earningspresentation.htm.jsonl, page 6; 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 36; Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A)

What would change the view upward is trailing EBITDA returning above the FY2025 level of USD 3,395 million with net leverage back below 5.73x, evidence that the net receivable from the parent is secured or repayable on set terms, and the 2028 maturities being refinanced early. What would change it downward is fuel staying near the outlook price into 2027 while growth slows as management expects, a card processor holdback, a restart of dividends or buybacks before leverage falls, or a further advance to the parent; each ten cents per gallon adds about USD 450 million to group annual fuel cost.
Basis: calculation N15; calculation N01; EX-99.2_2026-10-22_earningspresentation.htm.jsonl, page 5; 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 253; Financial foundation (CP-1)
### Limitations

- Reported EBITDA is derived from statement lines and omits depreciation booked in other lines, so the leverage and cover conclusions overstate leverage and understate cover, by an amount that the sources allow to be sized only for FY2025, where total leverage would be about 0.59x lower.
Basis: calculation N18; Financial foundation (CP-1)

- No credit ratings, market prices or peer figures were supplied, so the conclusion that credit quality is constrained is not placed against the sector or the market and could move either way once those are known.

- No executed debt documents were supplied, so the liquidity and refinancing conclusions rest on the issuer's summaries and no covenant headroom, ranking or legal capacity is assessed; a tighter covenant than summarised would weaken the liquidity conclusion.
- The 2026 interim cash flow statements are year-to-date and omit working capital lines, so the cash conversion conclusion for 2026 is qualitative about what drove operating cash flow.
- Nothing after 2026-10-22 is in the sources, so the fourth-quarter fuel and demand outcome is unknown and the downside path is a scenario built on management's stated assumptions, not a forecast.
### Strengths and weaknesses

Strengths. The first is liquidity: USD 11,763 million is available with no revolver drawing and facility maturities extended to 2031, which gives time to absorb a fuel or demand shock. The second is loyalty and co-brand income at 13.82% of FY2025 revenue, a stream less tied to fares than ticket sales, although it is pledged to AAdvantage lenders. The third is policy: no dividends or buybacks in 2025 or 2024 and no sponsor. The fourth is maturity management in 2026, including the 2014 term loan moved to May 2033, which removed a January 2027 maturity. The fifth is scale: a mainline fleet of which 54.00% is owned and a hub network that management says is carrying premium and corporate growth.
Basis: calculation N08; calculation N16; calculation N17; Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 100

Weaknesses. The first is leverage of 6.04x net on derived EBITDA with cover of 2.06x, which leaves little room for a further earnings decline. The second is unhedged fuel, which took operating margin to 1.14%. The third is the receivable from the parent of USD 10,430 million, above American's equity. The fourth is encumbrance: all principal is secured and USD 870 million was added junior on financed aircraft. The fifth is cash conversion, with a trailing free cash flow deficit of USD 132 million while fleet commitments continue.
Basis: calculation N01; calculation N02; calculation N06; calculation N13; calculation N19; calculation N11; Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A)

### Business, ownership and revenue drivers

American is a major network carrier that sells scheduled passenger and cargo transportation through nine hubs, buys regional capacity from wholly-owned and third-party carriers at fixed fees, and earns a loyalty and co-brand income stream alongside ticket revenue. The credit link is mixed: passenger travel is 83.49% of FY2025 revenue and is discretionary and cyclical, so cash-flow visibility comes mainly from the 13.82% loyalty share and from advance ticket sales, and refinancing confidence rests on a secured funding market that American used repeatedly in 2026.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 9; 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 10; 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 211

Ownership is simple: American is wholly owned by a widely held parent with no sponsor, foreign ownership caps and a tax plan that deters concentrated holders. The credit implications are low extraction risk and no sponsor support to count on; the exposure runs the other way, through the net receivable from the parent, and legal capacity to move cash cannot be read without the executed debt documents.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 102; 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 104; 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 40

Revenue is driven by volume and fare on a domestic base of 70.91% of FY2025 passenger revenue, with growth in Atlantic and Pacific flying and in premium products. Pricing power is limited because fares are set against competing network, low-cost and ultra-low-cost carriers that match price cuts quickly, which means higher fuel cost cannot be assumed to pass through to fares. The loyalty stream is the least cyclical part of revenue, and the 10-year Mastercard agreement and the Citibank exclusivity from 2026 add contractual visibility.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 13; 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 15; 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 211
### Cost structure, margin and cash conversion

Costs are largely fixed or outside management control in the short run. Fuel was 26.49% of revenue in nine months of 2026 against 19.73% a year earlier, salaries and benefits are the largest line with 87% of employees under collective agreements, and regional capacity is bought at predetermined fees with fuel and airport costs reimbursed. Operating leverage is therefore high: margin fell to 1.14% from 2.56% on a 15.63% revenue rise, and it cannot be defended against a fuel shock without capacity or fare action.
Basis: calculation N06; calculation N04; Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 25; 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 253

Capital intensity is high and only partly flexible. Capital expenditure and aircraft purchase deposits were USD 2,660 million in nine months and definitive orders extend beyond 2029, but management reduced its 2026 delivery plan from 55 to 49 aircraft and capital expenditure to about USD 4 billion at group level, which shows some flexibility over the maturity wall. Free cash flow conversion is poor on a trailing basis, and the seasonal float and federal tax losses of about USD 11.7 billion flatter cash flow, because ticket and mileage cash reverses and the tax shield is not permanent.

Basis: calculation N11; calculation N14; Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 64; 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 36; EX-99.2_2026-04-23_earningspresentation.htm.jsonl, page 6
### Competitive and macro forces

Rivalry is intense and sets pricing, because carriers match fare cuts quickly and ultra-low-cost carriers press fares in many markets, which limits margin recovery when costs rise. The threat of new entrants is moderated by hub, slot and gate constraints that the annual report describes and by aircraft supply, and substitutes matter mainly on short segments where ground and rail compete. Buyer power sits with corporate accounts and online travel agents that control distribution and its cost, and supplier power is high because a limited number of manufacturers supply aircraft and engines, delaying deliveries or raising fleet cost, while unions and fuel suppliers set the two largest costs.

Macro and policy factors are material here, unlike in many sectors. Conflict in the Middle East and Ukraine has contributed to oil price volatility, which feeds straight into fuel cost, and a prolonged government shutdown, regulation of routes and slots, and antitrust litigation over the Northeast Alliance can each change earnings or cash. These matter to credit because fuel is the main cause of the margin squeeze and because litigation cash calls compete with debt service.

In credit terms the strengths are liquidity, loyalty income, payout policy, extended maturities and an owned fleet; the weaknesses are leverage, unhedged fuel, the parent receivable, pledged assets and weak cash conversion. The opportunities are fuel prices easing, premium and loyalty growth that management reports, and fleet renewal that lowers unit cost; the threats are a sustained fuel shock, labour contract resets in 2027, litigation and a stressed parent.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); EX-99.2_2026-10-22_earningspresentation.htm.jsonl, page 5
### Financial profile and outlook

The financial profile reads as follows, dimension by dimension. Scale and market position are strong, with a mainline fleet of more than 1,000 aircraft and revenue of USD 54,626 million in FY2025. Competitive advantage and business diversification are average, because hubs and loyalty income are offset by fare competition and a domestic base. Cost and capex flexibility, margin stability and free cash flow stability are weak, for the reasons above. Ability to refinance is average: secured access is proven but the issuer carries a non-investment grade rating, and USD 7,861 million falls due in 2028. Liquidity is strong at USD 11,763 million. Financial policy and governance are average, because payouts are conservative while the parent receivable is large and legal capacity is unread.
Basis: calculation N08; calculation N10; calculation N06; Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 33

Over the next 12 to 24 months management guides at group level to fourth-quarter revenue growth of 19.5% to 22.5% and a full-year 2026 adjusted loss per share of USD 1.00 to USD 1.60, on a fuel price of about USD 4.70 per gallon and a fuel cost headwind of about USD 7 billion for the year, and says growth will slow in 2027 amid elevated fuel prices. The headwinds are fuel, labour resets and fleet spending; the tailwinds are premium, corporate and loyalty growth and the secured financing market. Medium-term outlook beyond 2027 is not established in the sources.
Basis: EX-99.2_2026-10-22_earningspresentation.htm.jsonl, page 5; EX-99.2_2026-10-22_earningspresentation.htm.jsonl, page 6
### Downside scenario

The scenario is a prolonged fuel shock rather than a recession. The initiating condition is fuel staying near the outlook price of about USD 4.70 per gallon through 2027 while growth slows, as management expects. The first operational break is that unit revenue gains fade but fuel, labour and fixed regional fees do not, so operating margin falls below 1.14% and EBITDA below the trailing USD 2,916 million; each ten cents per gallon adds about USD 450 million to group annual fuel cost. Financial transmission follows: net leverage rises above 6.04x, cover falls below 2.06x, and free cash flow stays negative while aircraft deliveries continue and the customer-funded float of USD 21,861 million reverses in a slower season.
Basis: calculation N15; calculation N01; calculation N14; Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 69; EX-99.2_2026-10-22_earningspresentation.htm.jsonl, page 6

The liquidity consequence is that USD 11,763 million of liquidity covers the USD 11,411 million of principal due in 2027 and 2028 only 1.03x, with cash also needed for operations, so a card processor holdback would matter. Management levers are real: capital expenditure and deliveries can be cut, as they were in 2026, aircraft certificates have repeatedly funded deliveries, sale-leasebacks have yielded USD 77 million in nine months, and repayment of part of the USD 10,430 million receivable by the parent is a possible lever although its terms are not established. Resilience appears sufficient to avoid liquidity distress through 2027 on stated liquidity, but the 2028 maturities of USD 7,861 million would need earnings recovery or continued secured market access, and an observable trigger is the refinancing of the 2028 notes and loans before leverage rises further. No default is assumed.

Basis: calculation N09; calculation N10; Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_aal-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 26; EX-99.2_2026-04-23_earningspresentation.htm.jsonl, page 6; 10-K_2025-12-31_aal-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 253
### Overall credit view

Overall, American presents an adequate business profile supported by liquidity, loyalty income, extended maturities and conservative payouts, but credit quality is constrained by fuel-driven margin compression, net leverage of 6.04x on derived EBITDA, a USD 10,430 million receivable from its parent and a largely pledged asset base. Cash-flow durability appears weak because trailing free cash flow is a deficit of USD 132 million. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on fuel prices and continued secured market access ahead of USD 7,861 million due in 2028. The primary downside path is a prolonged fuel shock on fixed labour, regional and fleet costs. Further analysis would require ratings, executed debt documents, the proxy statement and the intercompany terms. Fundamental credit completed. Top risk: sustained fuel cost without margin recovery.
